correctness.rationale: For a fixed finite allowed-degree set S, an X-prime jump decides each Sigma^0_1(X) question “there exist at least j successors” for all 1≤j≤max S, giving exact finite rows and a uniform recursive valuation for every formula. Singleton S={k} needs no jump since the known k-successor search terminates in X, including k=0. For S containing k<ell, build X-computable frame with k common successors per world and ell−k optional dummy successors at testing world s_e iff machine e first halts at one stage. The first-halting predicate at fixed t is X-decidable, so R exists in RCA0. Design p false on dummy and true on the common successors; at s_e the depth-one formula ¬□p codes X′. Therefore every valuation yields X′, giving ACA0, and the upper bound proves the converse and exact 0′ degree for a computable witness. No finite test purports to verify all oracles, indices, or formulas.

value.rationale: The result identifies a natural, complete reverse-mathematical phase transition: prescribing exactly one successor count makes all modal valuations computable, whereas permitting any two different counts forces arithmetical comprehension. Sharp depth-one coding and Turing-jump complexity yield a useful exact boundary, not merely a relabeling of a given fixed numerical example. The proof is short but the all-spectrum classification is naturally motivated.
